summary: HDFC Bank provides accounts for keeping and moving money, loans for homes and other needs, and services for businesses.
description: Imagine a household saving money and another household borrowing to buy a home. HDFC Bank serves both. It accepts money in accounts, makes loans, holds investments and processes payments. It must keep serving withdrawals while collecting repayments over time.
money: Borrowers pay interest for using money and customers pay fees for some services. The bank also earns interest on investments. From this income it pays interest on deposits and other borrowing, staff and technology costs, and charges for loans that may not be repaid. A deposit received is money the bank owes the customer, not profit.
customers: A home buyer pays loan interest; a cardholder may pay applicable interest and fees; a business pays for borrowing or services such as handling payments. Savers may receive interest from the bank. One customer can use several of these services.
drivers: Whether borrowers repay, what the bank earns on loans and investments, what it pays for funding, the cost of serving customers, and whether enough money is available when payments fall due.

groups.title: Accounts: keep and move money
groups.examples: Savings and current accounts, fixed and recurring deposits.
groups.explanation: Customers deposit money and use accounts to save, receive income or make payments. Fixed deposits keep money for an agreed period. The bank owes these balances to customers under the account terms.

groups.title: Household loans and credit cards
groups.examples: Home, vehicle and personal loans, and credit cards.
groups.explanation: A borrower receives money now and repays it under agreed terms. A credit card lets a customer pay for purchases using credit. Interest and relevant fees help cover the bank’s funding, service costs and repayment risk.

groups.title: Loans and payment services for businesses
groups.examples: Business loans, finance for daily operations, trade payments and collections.
groups.explanation: A shop may need money to buy stock before customers pay. A larger company may need a longer-term loan or help paying suppliers. The bank checks repayment ability and charges for the loan or service.

groups.title: Investments and products supplied by others
groups.examples: Bank investments and distribution of financial products.
groups.explanation: The bank invests some money and can help customers buy products from other providers. A fee for arranging an insurance or investment product is different from receiving all the money that provider earns.

basics.title: What part of a repayment is income?
basics.text: Returning the amount borrowed, called principal, gives the bank its money back. Interest is the extra amount charged for using that money. The whole loan repayment is not revenue or profit.

basics.title: What happens when a borrower may not repay?
basics.text: The bank records a charge or allowance for possible loan losses, called a provision. A problem loan is not necessarily a complete loss: some money may still be recovered. Property pledged against a loan can help recovery, but selling it can take time.

steps.title: Offer accounts and arrange funding
steps.text: The bank serves depositors and can borrow through other permitted routes. These sources have different costs and repayment terms.

steps.title: Check the borrower and agree a loan
steps.text: It examines income, existing debts and any property pledged as security before agreeing the amount, interest and repayment schedule.

steps.title: Run accounts and collect repayments
steps.text: Customers use payment services. Borrowers pay principal and interest; the bank pays deposit interest and its staff, systems and other bills.

steps.title: Handle late payments and keep money available
steps.text: It follows up overdue loans, records expected losses and keeps funds available for withdrawals and other obligations.

specifics.title: The interest difference still has costs to cover
specifics.text: Interest earned minus interest paid is called net interest income. It still has to help cover branches, people, technology, loan losses and tax. A larger interest income total does not automatically mean a larger profit.

specifics.title: More loans need dependable funding
specifics.text: Home loans can be repaid over a long time, while some account balances can be withdrawn quickly. The bank must manage that timing difference and the price it pays to attract deposits.

specifics.title: Financial strength and ready cash answer different questions
specifics.text: Capital is the bank’s cushion for absorbing losses. Liquidity means being able to make payments when due. A bank needs both; earning a profit alone does not establish that either is sufficient.

watch: Can the bank fund its growing loans?
Deposits and other borrowing must remain available at a workable cost.
Compare lending with deposit balances, other borrowing and the interest paid for funding. Check whether growth depends increasingly on expensive deposits or borrowing.
What is changing the interest difference?
Loan interest and deposit interest can change at different times.

Read the explanation of loan rates, deposit costs and loan types. If using net interest margin, check its definition: it compares net interest income with a stated average amount of assets, such as loans and investments, rather than showing final profit.
New loans can develop problems later.

Check newly identified problem loans, repayments recovered and provisions for losses. Read the amount of troubled loans as well as its share of total lending; rapid new lending can make that share look smaller.
Are services earning enough to cover their costs?
Busy payment channels still cost money to operate.
Compare fees with staff, branch and technology spending. Check which products the bank supplies itself and which it only helps another provider sell.
Are the bank and the wider group being compared correctly?
Subsidiaries can add businesses with different costs.
Standalone accounts cover the bank itself; consolidated accounts include controlled companies. Use each consistently, and check capital and money available for payments alongside earnings.
risks: Lost jobs, business difficulties or lower sale proceeds from pledged property can increase losses.
The bank may need to pay more for deposits or find other money to meet withdrawals and fund loans.
Interest rates change at different times
What the bank pays for deposits can rise before what it earns from existing loans.
System outages, fraud, cyber incidents or rule breaches can cost money and damage customer trust.
context: The work continues after a loan is approved. Repayments and signs of difficulty need monitoring throughout its life; lending quickly today can create losses that appear later.
quiz: Is a home-loan repayment entirely income for the bank?
No. The principal returns the money lent. Interest is income, but funding costs, running costs, loan losses and tax still have to be covered before profit remains.

financialNotes.title: Verify banking measures on the same basis
financialNotes.text: The table pairs consolidated group total income with profit after tax attributable to owners. Total income is before funding, insurance, operating and credit-loss costs, and is different from net interest income. Deposit and loan balances are not revenue. Use the standalone bank accounts separately when investigating lending spreads and provisions.
